Remote-Sensing Data, Provenance, and Vegetation Indices

bayesAgriFlow

Source: vignettes/v36-remote-sensing-data-and-indices.Rmd
v36-remote-sensing-data-and-indices.Rmd

Purpose

Version 1.3.0 adds an analysis-ready remote-sensing layer without turning bayesAgriFlow into an image-processing package. Orthomosaic generation, radiometric calibration, atmospheric correction, georegistration, cloud masking, and other sensor-specific preprocessing should occur in specialist software before Bayesian modeling. The package begins where scientific variables are ready to be linked to experimental units, coordinates, acquisition times, and reference measurements. UAV phenotyping can greatly increase throughput, but useful inference still depends on experimental structure and calibration to the biological target (Yang et al. 2017).

The guiding distinction is:

raw imagery -> specialist preprocessing -> analysis-ready features -> Bayesian model -> posterior decision quantity

1. Analysis-ready means auditable

An analysis-ready table should retain enough metadata to reconstruct where every feature came from. A vegetation index without platform, date, spatial support, preprocessing notes, and experimental-unit identity is easy to misuse. bayes_rs_data() therefore stores roles and provenance rather than hiding the input behind an opaque image object.

d <- bayes_teaching_data("uav")
rs <- bayes_rs_data(
  d, x_coord = "x", y_coord = "y", id = "plot_id",
  source = "uav",
  metadata = list(platform = "simulated UAV", unit = "plot")
)
print(rs)

Interpretation checklist

  • Keep raw-image preprocessing outside the statistical model unless its uncertainty is modeled explicitly.
  • Preserve plot or pixel identifiers so repeated measurements can be traced.
  • Record the coordinate reference system when coordinates are spatial.
  • Treat provenance as part of reproducibility, not decoration.

2. Input representations

The core model works with ordinary data frames. When terra is installed, a SpatRaster may be converted or sampled explicitly. sf is accepted only through the optional extraction route. These packages remain in Suggests, so users who work only with plot-level features do not inherit geospatial dependencies.

# Tabular route
rs_tab <- bayes_rs_data(d, "x", "y", id = "plot_id", source = "uav")

# Optional raster route
if (FALSE) {
  rs_raster <- bayes_rs_data(r, source = "satellite")
}

Interpretation checklist

  • Prefer a table when the inferential unit is the plot.
  • Use raster objects when spatially continuous outputs are genuinely required.
  • Do not duplicate raster values merely to make a model look spatial.

3. Raster extraction is a scientific operation

bayes_rs_extract() is intentionally thin. Point extraction can use nearest-cell or bilinear interpolation. Polygon extraction can summarize cells over experimental plots. The extraction method changes the meaning and support of the resulting predictor, so it must be documented.

if (FALSE) {
  plot_features <- bayes_rs_extract(
    raster = index_stack,
    locations = plot_polygons,
    fun = "mean", exact = TRUE
  )
  point_features <- bayes_rs_extract(
    raster = index_stack,
    locations = sampling_points,
    method = "bilinear"
  )
}

Interpretation checklist

  • A polygon mean is not equivalent to a center-pixel value.
  • Bilinear interpolation creates a local weighted value rather than a measured pixel.
  • Check CRS alignment before extraction in the upstream geospatial workflow.

4. Vegetation indices are transformations, not traits

Vegetation indices compress spectral bands into interpretable contrasts, but they are not direct measurements of biomass, nitrogen status, or yield. The review by Xue and Su emphasizes that vegetation indices vary in sensitivity to canopy, soil, atmospheric, and sensor conditions (Xue and Su 2017). Version 1.3.0 supplies NDVI, EVI, SAVI, and NDRE as transparent calculations.

z <- bayes_rs_indices(
  d, nir = "nir", red = "red", blue = "blue",
  red_edge = "red_edge",
  indices = c("NDVI", "EVI", "SAVI", "NDRE")
)
head(z[c("rs_ndvi", "rs_evi", "rs_savi", "rs_ndre")])

Interpretation checklist

  • State which reflectance bands were used.
  • Do not compare index values from incompatible preprocessing pipelines without justification.
  • Keep index equations separate from the biological calibration model.

5. NDVI

NDVI contrasts near-infrared and red reflectance. It is bounded when reflectances are non-negative, but saturation and denominator behavior still matter. bayes_rs_indices() returns missing values when the denominator is effectively zero instead of silently generating infinite values.

ndvi_only <- bayes_rs_indices(d, nir = "nir", red = "red", indices = "NDVI")
summary(ndvi_only$rs_ndvi)

Interpretation checklist

  • Inspect the observed range before specifying priors.
  • Do not interpret the index scale as the response scale.
  • Check for extreme values created by poor reflectance measurements.

6. EVI, SAVI, and NDRE

EVI uses the blue band in addition to NIR and red; SAVI introduces an explicit soil-adjustment constant; NDRE replaces red with a red-edge band. Their inputs are therefore not interchangeable. The function requires the relevant bands rather than guessing them.

z2 <- bayes_rs_indices(d, "nir", "red", blue = "blue", red_edge = "red_edge", L = 0.5)
summary(z2[c("rs_evi", "rs_savi", "rs_ndre")])

Interpretation checklist

  • Treat the SAVI constant as a scientific choice.
  • Require the blue band for EVI and red-edge band for NDRE.
  • Use multiple indices only when they contribute information rather than redundant columns.

7. Pixel support versus experimental unit

Agricultural experiments are randomized at experimental-unit levels, not at individual image pixels merely because millions of pixels are available. If many pixels belong to one plot, treating them as independent replicates creates pseudoreplication. Version 1.3.0 encourages plot-level extraction or explicit hierarchical modeling.

# Prefer a plot-level table when the treatment was randomized by plot.
plot_rs <- bayes_rs_data(d, "x", "y", id = "plot_id")

Interpretation checklist

  • Identify the randomization unit before selecting the remote-sensing support.
  • Use pixels as repeated or nested measurements when appropriate, not independent treatment replicates.
  • Match prediction scale to the scientific question.

8. Missing imagery and quality flags

Cloud, shadow, flight gaps, calibration failures, and segmentation errors can create structured missingness. A clean table should retain quality flags upstream. bayesAgriFlow can later use its missing-data workflows, but deletion or imputation should never erase the acquisition mechanism.

# Quality filtering is explicit and happens before the model.
quality_ok <- subset(d, is.finite(ndvi))

Interpretation checklist

  • Document why observations are missing.
  • Distinguish sensor failure from biological absence.
  • Consider sensitivity analysis if missingness may be informative.

9. Coordinate roles

Coordinates are optional unless a spatial model is requested. When supplied, they should represent a metric or scientifically defensible geometry for the chosen Gaussian-process model. Degrees of longitude and latitude should not automatically be treated as Euclidean meters.

rs_xy <- bayes_rs_data(d, x_coord = "x", y_coord = "y", id = "plot_id")
rs_xy$roles

Interpretation checklist

  • Check coordinate units.
  • Use projected coordinates for local field-distance models when appropriate.
  • Do not infer spatial dependence solely from the presence of coordinates.

10. Acquisition time roles

Time can be numeric, Date, or POSIX time. Remote-sensing models convert Date/POSIX acquisitions to elapsed days while retaining the original time column for provenance. This supports later temporal structures without losing the acquisition calendar.

sat <- bayes_teaching_data("satellite")
rs_time <- bayes_rs_data(sat, "x", "y", time = "day", source = "satellite")
rs_time$roles

Interpretation checklist

  • Use elapsed time when temporal distance matters.
  • Preserve original acquisition dates in the dataset.
  • Do not assume irregular acquisitions are equally spaced.

11. Data dictionaries

Each remote-sensing teaching dataset is simulated and should be accompanied by a data dictionary in a real analysis. At minimum, units are needed for response, bands, heights, temperatures, and coordinate variables. A column name such as height is insufficient without stating whether it is centimeters, meters, or a normalized canopy metric.

names(bayes_teaching_data("uav"))
names(bayes_teaching_data("satellite"))

Interpretation checklist

  • Record units in project metadata.
  • State whether bands are reflectance, digital numbers, or transformed values.
  • Keep sensor-derived predictors distinguishable from ground-reference outcomes.

12. Pre-fit exploratory checks

Exploration should focus on scale, missingness, replication, and relationships that affect model specification. It should not be used to repeatedly search for a model that produces a desired inferential conclusion.

summary(d[c("ndvi", "ndre", "canopy_height", "biomass")])
table(d$block)

Interpretation checklist

  • Inspect distributions before choosing priors.
  • Check replicate counts by treatment and block.
  • Look for impossible sensor values.
  • Separate exploratory plots from confirmatory model decisions.

13. What the package deliberately does not automate

Version 1.3.0 does not automatically orthorectify imagery, classify clouds, segment plants, choose spectral features, resample rasters, or select a coordinate reference system. These steps are sensor- and project-specific and deserve explicit specialist workflows.

Interpretation checklist

  • Do not interpret absence of automation as absence of importance.
  • Freeze upstream preprocessing settings alongside the Bayesian analysis.
  • Version processed imagery and extracted tables together.

14. Reproducibility contract

A reproducible remote-sensing Bayesian analysis should be able to move from a frozen feature table to a declared design, prior, fit, diagnostic record, posterior prediction, and map-ready product. The raw imagery can be archived separately when it is too large for an R package example.

des <- bayes_rs_model(
  d, response = "biomass", predictors = c("ndvi", "canopy_height"),
  x_coord = "x", y_coord = "y", block = "block"
)
bayes_plan(des)

Interpretation checklist

  • Freeze the analysis-ready table.
  • Record software versions and random seeds.
  • Keep heavy backends optional and declared.
  • Archive the mapping from imagery to plot identifiers.

15. Transition to modeling

The next vignette moves from data provenance to Bayesian phenotyping models. The key principle is that image-derived features enter the model as measurements with experimental structure, not as intrinsically independent observations.

des <- bayes_rs_phenotype(
  d, trait = "biomass", features = c("ndvi", "ndre", "canopy_height"),
  x_coord = "x", y_coord = "y", block = "block"
)
bayes_plan(des)

Interpretation checklist

  • Carry experimental design information into the model.
  • Use measurement-error inputs when known sensor uncertainty is available.
  • Interpret posterior predictions on the biological response scale.

End-to-end checklist

  1. Complete sensor-specific preprocessing outside the package.
  2. Freeze an analysis-ready table or raster product.
  3. Record source, coordinates, time, experimental-unit identifiers, and units.
  4. Calculate only scientifically justified indices.
  5. Extract pixel information at the correct experimental support.
  6. Carry measurement uncertainty forward when it is known.
  7. Declare the design before fitting.
  8. Distinguish interpolation, extrapolation, and biological calibration.
  9. Report posterior uncertainty, not only fitted maps.
  10. Archive provenance with the analysis.

Practical audit worksheet

Use the following questions before freezing an analysis-ready remote-sensing dataset.

  1. What physical quantity does each spectral band represent?
  2. Were digital numbers converted to reflectance, and by which workflow?
  3. Which coordinate reference system is used?
  4. What is the spatial support of one table row?
  5. Which experimental unit received the randomized treatment?
  6. Are multiple pixels nested within the same experimental unit?
  7. Which acquisition date or time belongs to each record?
  8. Were clouds, shadows, or low-quality pixels removed?
  9. Which quality flags were retained?
  10. Which vegetation-index equations were applied?
  11. Are sensor and biological response units documented?
  12. Can every feature be traced to the upstream imagery?
  13. Are missing observations distinguishable from zero measurements?
  14. Is the prediction domain represented by the training domain?
  15. Is there a frozen data dictionary and provenance record?

A satisfactory answer to these questions is part of the statistical analysis because it determines what the model variables mean.

Xue, Jinru, and Baofeng Su. 2017. “Significant Remote Sensing Vegetation Indices: A Review of Developments and Applications.” Journal of Sensors 2017: 1–17. https://doi.org/10.1155/2017/1353691.
Yang, Guijun, Jiangang Liu, Chunjiang Zhao, et al. 2017. “Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Remote Sensing for Field-Based Crop Phenotyping: Current Status and Perspectives.” Frontiers in Plant Science 8: 1111. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2017.01111.
